behavior_items: The bug report describes a Fortran SELECT TYPE construct whose selector is a polymorphic pointer component expression, specifically a form like `select type (ap => tp%ptr)` where `tp%ptr` is a pointer component that can later be redirected.

Before entering the SELECT TYPE, a call such as `call tp%setref(i)` makes the component pointer `tp%ptr` point at target `i`. At selector establishment time, the dynamic object designated by `tp%ptr` is therefore `i`.

Inside the SELECT TYPE block, execution reaches `class default`, meaning the test is not about type resolution differences but about the association semantics of the local selector name `ap` after the construct has already been entered.

Within that block, another call such as `call tp%setref(j)` changes `tp%ptr` so that the component pointer now points at a different target `j`. This mutation occurs after `ap` was introduced by the SELECT TYPE header.

The critical question exercised by the reproducer is whether `ap` remains bound to the original selected object from construct entry, or whether every later use of `ap` is effectively re-evaluated through the current state of `tp%ptr`.

The report’s expected interpretation is that the associate name in `select type (ap => tp%ptr)` should bind to the selected polymorphic entity at the moment the construct is entered, not act as a live alias for the pointer component expression itself.

The next operation, `lp => ap`, tests that interpretation directly. If `ap` is a stable association to the original target `i`, then `lp` should become associated with `i` even though `tp%ptr` has meanwhile been redirected to `j`.

A later call such as `call set7(lp)` writes through `lp`. Therefore the final observable program state distinguishes the two semantics unambiguously: writing `7` through `lp` should affect either `i` or `j`, depending on what `ap` denotes.

Gfortran 8.2 reportedly prints `I: 3` and `J: 7`, which shows that `lp => ap` ultimately followed the updated `tp%ptr` and modified `j` rather than `i`. This means the compiler treated `ap` as if it were tied to the mutable pointer component reference, not to the originally selected object.

Intel Fortran reportedly prints `I: 7` and `J: 4`, which shows that `lp => ap` remained associated with the original object selected on entry to the construct. In that execution, changing `tp%ptr` later did not retarget `ap`.

Thus the reproducer isolates a compiler semantic issue in association handling for SELECT TYPE with a polymorphic selector that is itself a pointer component expression and that gets reassigned inside the construct.

The exercised compiler behavior is not about optimization, code generation crashes, or parsing; it is about front-end semantic lowering and runtime association model: whether the compiler materializes a snapshot binding for the associate name or leaves it as a deferred reference to the original selector expression.

According to the bug report discussion, the correct behavior is the snapshot-style binding: `ap` should denote the entity selected when the construct begins. Under that reading, gfortran’s output is incorrect because it effectively rebinds `ap` after `tp%ptr` changes.

So the reproducer is a minimal aliasing/association test: establish pointer to `i`, enter SELECT TYPE and name it `ap`, mutate the underlying pointer component to point to `j`, copy `ap` into another pointer `lp`, assign through `lp`, and inspect whether `i` or `j` changed.

The failure demonstrates that GCC mishandles local-name association in SELECT TYPE when the selector is a mutable polymorphic pointer component, causing later references to the local name to track pointer reseating when they should continue to designate the original selected target.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: The reproducer targets GCC Fortran’s handling of `select type (ap => tp%ptr)` when `tp%ptr` is a polymorphic pointer component that is reassigned inside the SELECT TYPE block. The program first makes `tp%ptr` point to `i`, enters the construct, then redirects `tp%ptr` to `j`, assigns `lp => ap`, and writes through `lp`. If the associate name `ap` is correctly bound to the selected entity at construct entry, `lp` should still point to `i`, producing Intel’s `I: 7, J: 4`. Gfortran instead produces `I: 3, J: 7`, showing it treated `ap` as if it were still tied to the mutable selector expression and therefore followed the updated pointer component. The reproducer therefore exercises incorrect association semantics in GCC’s SELECT TYPE implementation.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The failure pattern is a Fortran front-end semantic/association bug in SELECT TYPE, specifically when the selector is a polymorphic pointer component expression such as `tp%ptr` and that component is reassigned after construct entry. The common pattern is: a selector designates target `i` at entry, a local selector name `ap` is introduced with `select type (ap => tp%ptr)`, the underlying pointer component is later redirected to `j`, and a subsequent pointer association `lp => ap` reveals whether `ap` was captured as the selected entity at entry or left as a live reference to the mutable selector expression. Gfortran's result shows `ap` tracked the later value of `tp%ptr`, which means GCC likely implemented the associate name as an alias to the selector expression or descriptor slot rather than as a stabilized binding to the selected object established on entry. This points to a defect in semantic lowering / resolution of SELECT TYPE associations, especially for pointer-component selectors with polymorphic descriptors.
possible_causes: Incorrect SELECT TYPE lowering: the associate name for `select type (ap => tp%ptr)` is represented as a reference to the original selector expression `tp%ptr` instead of a temporary snapshot of the selected entity taken at construct entry.

Wrong handling of pointer-component selectors in the Fortran front end: reassignment of `tp%ptr` updates the descriptor/storage later reused for `ap`, so uses of `ap` effectively re-fetch the current pointer target rather than preserving the original one.

Missing temporary descriptor or saved association record for polymorphic selector expressions in SELECT TYPE, causing the local name to alias the mutable selector component instead of the selected object.

Bug in resolution/trans-expr code for associate/select-type names where pointer association semantics are confused with expression aliasing semantics, especially for component references and class-wide polymorphic pointers.

Incorrect descriptor copy-vs-reference choice for class/polymorphic entities: GCC may be sharing a descriptor for `ap` with `tp%ptr` rather than cloning/binding it, so later pointer reseating of `tp%ptr` retargets `ap`.
Fault in generated runtime association metadata for CLASS DEFAULT block entry, where the selected entity is not materialized independently before executing the block.
Symbol table / namespace binding bug for the local selector name in SELECT TYPE causing later references to resolve back to the selector expression tree instead of a dedicated construct-local entity.

Potential mishandling of pointer-valued component references in SELECT TYPE compared with ASSOCIATE, suggesting shared compiler code does not correctly distinguish selecting the current designated object from tracking the pointer component itself.
evidence: The selector is a polymorphic pointer component expression `tp%ptr`, not a simple variable, and the bug only manifests after that component is redirected inside the construct.
At construct entry `tp%ptr` points to `i`, so a correct entry-time binding should make later `lp => ap` associate with `i` even after `tp%ptr` is changed.
Inside the SELECT TYPE block, `call tp%setref(j)` mutates only the component pointer, providing a direct test of whether `ap` is stable or live.
Observed gfortran output `I: 3, J: 7` proves that writing through `lp => ap` modified `j`, meaning `ap` followed the updated `tp%ptr` rather than the original selected object.
Comparison output from Intel Fortran `I: 7, J: 4` matches the expected snapshot-binding interpretation described in the report.
The issue is semantic, not parsing or optimization: type resolution reaches `class default`, and the wrong behavior concerns association identity after entry to the construct.

The report explicitly states the associate name should bind to the polymorphic entity at the point of definition, which aligns with the observed discrepancy and implicates GCC's implementation of local-name association in SELECT TYPE.

Following code will generate infinite loop in case where TO is INT_MAX (for +1 step) or INT_MIN (for -1 step) We translate a do loop from: DO dovar = from, to, step body END DO to: [Evaluate loop bounds and step] dovar = from; for (;;) { if (dovar > to) goto end_label; body; cycle_label: dovar += step; } end_label: This helps the optimizers by avoiding the extra pre-header condition and we save a register as we just compare the updated IV (not a value in previous step).

Translate the DO construct. This obviously is one of the most important ones to get right with any compiler, but especially so for Fortran. We special case some loop forms as described in gfc_trans_simple_do. For other cases we implement them with a separate loop count, as described in the standard. We translate a do loop from: DO dovar = from, to, step body END DO to: [evaluate loop bounds and step] empty = (step > 0 ? to < from : to > from); countm1 = (to - from) / step; dovar = from; if (empty) goto exit_label; for (;;) { body; cycle_label: dovar += step countm1t = countm1; countm1--; if (countm1t == 0) goto exit_label; } exit_label: countm1 is an unsigned integer. It is equal to the loop count minus one, because the loop count itself can overflow.

Translate the DO WHILE construct. We translate DO WHILE (cond) body END DO to: for ( ; ; ) { pre_cond; if (! cond) goto exit_label; body; cycle_label: } exit_label: Because the evaluation of the exit condition `cond' may have side effects, we can't do much for empty loop bodies. The backend optimizers should be smart enough to eliminate any dead loops.

Translate the SELECT CASE construct for INTEGER case expressions, without killing all potential optimizations. The problem is that Fortran allows unbounded cases, but the back-end does not, so we need to intercept those before we enter the equivalent SWITCH_EXPR we can build. For example, we translate this, SELECT CASE (expr) CASE (:100,101,105:115) block_1 CASE (190:199,200:) block_2 CASE (300) block_3 CASE DEFAULT block_4 END SELECT to the GENERIC equivalent, switch (expr) { case (minimum value for typeof(expr) ... 100: case 101: case 105 ... 114: block1: goto end_label; case 200 ... (maximum value for typeof(expr): case 190 ... 199: block2; goto end_label; case 300: block_3; goto end_label; default: block_4; goto end_label; } end_label:

Translate the SELECT CASE construct for LOGICAL case expressions. There are only two cases possible here, even though the standard does allow three cases in a LOGICAL SELECT CASE construct: .TRUE., .FALSE., and DEFAULT. We never generate more than two blocks here. Instead, we always try to eliminate the DEFAULT case. This way, we can translate this kind of SELECT construct to a simple if {} else {}; expression in GENERIC.

Translate the SELECT CASE construct for CHARACTER case expressions. Instead of generating compares and jumps, it is far simpler to generate a data structure describing the cases in order and call a library subroutine that locates the right case. This is particularly true because this is the only case where we might have to dispose of a temporary. The library subroutine returns a pointer to jump to or NULL if no branches are to be taken.

Translate the three variants of the SELECT CASE construct. SELECT CASEs with INTEGER case expressions can be translated to an equivalent GENERIC switch statement, and for LOGICAL case expressions we build one or two if-else compares. SELECT CASEs with CHARACTER case expressions are a whole different story, because they don't exist in GENERIC. So we sort them and do a binary search at runtime. Fortran has no BREAK statement, and it does not allow jumps from one case block to another. That makes things a lot easier for the optimizers.

Given a completely parsed select statement, we: - Validate all expressions and code within the SELECT. - Make sure that the selection expression is not of the wrong type. - Make sure that no case ranges overlap. - Eliminate unreachable cases and unreachable code resulting from removing case labels. The standard does allow unreachable cases, e.g. CASE (5:3). But they are a hassle for code generation, and to prevent that, we just cut them out here. This is not necessary for overlapping cases because they are illegal and we never even try to generate code. We have the additional caveat that a SELECT construct could have been a computed GOTO in the source code. Fortunately we can fairly easily work around that here: The case_expr for a "real" SELECT CASE is in code->expr1, but for a computed GOTO it is in code->expr2. gcc/builtins.cc.signature: static tree do_mpfr_lgamma_r (tree arg, tree arg_sg, tree type)
gcc/builtins.cc.summary: If ARG is a REAL_CST, call mpfr_lgamma() on it and return the resulting value as a tree with type TYPE. The mpfr precision is set to the precision of TYPE. We assume that this mpfr function returns zero if the result could be calculated exactly within the requested precision. In addition, the integer pointer represented by ARG_SG will be dereferenced and set to the appropriate signgam (-1,1) value.
